provenance: FORECAST / AI-GENERATED. Not a previous-year question.

questions.question: A, B and C are independent events with $\operatorname{P}(A) = 1/2, \operatorname{P}(B) = 1/3$ and $\operatorname{P}(C) = 1/4$. What is $\operatorname{P}\!\left(\text{at least one of them occurs}\right)$?
tips: Independence passes to the complements, so $\operatorname{P}\!\left(\text{none}\right)$ is always the product of the $(1 - p_{i})$.
Adding $1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 = 13/12$ exceeds 1; option (d) $13/24$ is that error halved and is planted for it.
solution: If A, B, C are independent then so are their complements.

questions.question: Ten persons sit at random around a round table. What is the probability that exactly 3 persons sit between A and B?
questions.shortcut: Fix A. B is equally likely to take any of the 9 remaining seats; 2 of them leave exactly 3 people between.
tips: At a round table always fix one person first; the other positions are then uniform on the remaining n - 1 seats.
"Exactly 3 between" counts BOTH arcs, clockwise and anticlockwise - forgetting one gives $1/9$, option (a).
solution: Fix A's seat; by symmetry B is uniform on the other 9 seats.
Exactly 3 people between A and B means B is 4 seats away clockwise or 4 seats away anticlockwise: 2 seats qualify.

questions.question: Two points are chosen independently and uniformly on $(0, 1)$. What is the probability that the distance between them is less than $1/2$?
questions.shortcut: The complement $\lvert X - Y\rvert \ge 1/2$ is two corner triangles of leg $1/2$: area $2(1/2)(1/2)^{2} = 1/4$. Answer $3/4$.
tips: Draw the unit square: $\lvert X - Y\rvert < c$ is the band around the diagonal, and its complement is two right triangles of leg 1 - c.
The band area $1 - (1 - c)^{2}$ is worth memorising; at $c = 1/2$ it gives $3/4$ immediately.
solution: The sample space is the unit square of area 1.
The event $\lvert X - Y\rvert \ge 1/2$ is the union of the triangles $y \le x - 1/2$ and $y \ge x + 1/2$, each of area $(1/2)(1/2)^{2} = 1/8$.

questions.question: X and Y are independent $U(0, 1)$ variables. What is the probability that the equation $t^{2} + 2$Xt + $Y = 0$ has real roots?
questions.shortcut: Real roots need the discriminant $4X^{2} - 4Y \ge 0$, i.e. $Y \le X^{2}$. Area under $y = x^{2}$ on $(0,1)$ is $1/3$.
tips: Reduce the algebra to a region in the unit square before integrating anything.
The middle coefficient is 2X, not X, so the discriminant is $4X^{2} - 4Y$ and the 4 cancels; using $X^{2} - 4Y$ instead gives $1/12$.
solution: Real roots require $X^{2} \ge Y, a$ region of the unit square.

questions.question: Five letters are placed at random into five addressed envelopes, one per envelope. What is the probability that no letter goes into its own envelope?
questions.shortcut: The number of derangements of 5 objects is 44, so the probability is $44/120 = 11/30$.
tips: The limit is $1/e = 0.3679$, and $11/30 = 0.3667$ is already within 0.002 of it - a fast sanity check.
solution: The total number of arrangements is $5! = 120$.

questions.question: If $\operatorname{P}(A) = 0.7$ and $\operatorname{P}(B) = 0.6$, the smallest possible value of $\operatorname{P}\!\left(A\ \text{intersect B}\right)$ is
questions.shortcut: $\operatorname{P}\!\left(A\ \text{union B}\right) \le 1$ forces $\operatorname{P}\!\left(A\ \text{and B}\right) \ge 0.7 + 0.6 - 1 = 0.3$.
tips: These are the Frechet bounds: $\max(0, p + q - 1) \le \operatorname{P}\!\left(A\ \text{and B}\right) \le \min(p, q)$.
0.42 is the independent value and 0 is the disjoint value; neither is attainable here because the two events must overlap.
solution: By the addition rule, $\operatorname{P}\!\left(A\ \text{union B}\right) = 0.7 + 0.6 - \operatorname{P}\!\left(A\ \text{and B}\right)$.
The bound is attained when A union B is the whole space, so the minimum is 0.3, option (b).

questions.question: Machines $M_{1}, M_{2}$ and $M_{3}$ produce 50%, 30% and 20% of the output with defect rates 2%, 3% and 4%. An item drawn at random is found defective. What is the probability that it came from $M_{3}$?
tips: Work in unnormalised weights - the common factor cancels and the arithmetic collapses to small integers.
The largest producer need not be the likeliest culprit; here $M_{1}$ gives $10/27$ and $M_{3}$ gives $8/27$ despite $M_{3}$ having the worst defect rate.
solution: The joint weights are $\operatorname{P}(M_{i})\operatorname{P}(D \mid M_{i})$: 0.010, 0.009 and 0.008.

questions.question: Urn 1 has 2 white and 3 black balls, urn 2 has 3 white and 2 black, urn 3 has 4 white and 1 black. An urn is chosen at random and one ball is drawn. What is the probability that it is white?
questions.shortcut: Equal urn totals, so just average the white counts: $(2 + 3 + 4)/(3 \times 5) = 9/15 = 3/5$.
tips: This is total probability, not Bayes - nothing is being inverted, so no posterior is needed.
When all urns hold the same number of balls the answer is the mean proportion; unequal totals would need weighting.

questions.question: A disease has prevalence 1%. A test has sensitivity 95% and specificity 90%. Given a positive test, what is the probability that the person has the disease?
tips: With a rare disease the false positives come from a huge healthy pool and swamp the true positives.

Sensitivity is $\operatorname{P}\!\left(\text{positive}\mid \text{disease}\right)$, NOT $\operatorname{P}\!\left(\text{disease}\mid \text{positive}\right)$; reporting 0.95 is the classic inversion error.

questions.question: Of four coins, three are fair and one is two-headed. One coin is chosen at random and tossed three times, giving three heads. What is the probability that the two-headed coin was chosen?
tips: Three heads is 8 times more likely under the two-headed coin, so the prior odds 1 : 3 become 8 : 3.
Each extra head multiplies the likelihood ratio by 2 - the posterior climbs fast with the number of tosses.

questions.question: What is the mode of the $\text{Binomial}(15, 0.4)$ distribution?
questions.shortcut: $(n + 1)p = 16(0.4) = 6.4$, not an integer, so the mode is $\operatorname{floor}(6.4) = 6$ and it is unique.
tips: The mode is $\operatorname{floor}((n+1)p)$; the mode is a tied pair only when $(n+1)p$ is an integer.
The mean $np = 6$ also happens to be 6 here, but that is a coincidence - never quote the mean as the mode.
solution: For the binomial, $\operatorname{P}(X = k)/\operatorname{P}(X = k-1) \ge 1$ exactly when $k \le (n+1)p$.
Since 6.4 is not an integer the mode is the unique value 6, option (b).

questions.question: X follows a Poisson distribution with $\operatorname{P}(X = 2) = \operatorname{P}(X = 3)$. What is $\operatorname{P}(X = 0)$?
questions.shortcut: $\operatorname{P}(X=3)/\operatorname{P}(X=2) = \lambda/3 = 1$ gives $\lambda = 3$, so $\operatorname{P}(X = 0) = e^{-3}$.
tips: The ratio of consecutive Poisson probabilities is $\lambda/k$ - the fastest route to $\lambda$ in every such question.
$\operatorname{P}(X = 0) = e^{-\lambda}$, never $\lambda e^{-\lambda}$; option (c) is that slip.

questions.question: X is geometric on {$1, 2, \ldots$} with success probability p and $q = 1 - p$. What is $\operatorname{P}(X > m + n \mid X > m)$?
questions.shortcut: Memorylessness: the conditional law of X - m given $X > m$ is the original geometric law, so the answer is $q^{n}$.
tips: $\operatorname{P}(X > k) = q^{k}$ for the geometric on {$1, 2, \ldots$}; the answer is that survival function at n.
The geometric is the ONLY memoryless discrete law, exactly as the exponential is the only continuous one.
solution: $\operatorname{P}(X > k) = q^{k}$ for a geometric on {$1, 2, \ldots$}.

questions.question: A fair coin is tossed repeatedly. What is the probability that the 5th head occurs on the 8th toss?
questions.shortcut: Negative binomial: $\binom{7}{4}(1/2)^{8} = 35/256$.
tips: The 8th toss must be a head, so choose the other 4 heads among the FIRST 7 tosses, not among all 8.
Using $\binom{8}{5}$ instead of $\binom{7}{4}$ gives $56/256$, planted as option (d).
solution: The 8th toss is a head, and exactly 4 of the first 7 tosses are heads.

questions.question: In a multinomial experiment with $n = 10$ and cell probabilities $(0.2, 0.3, 0.5)$, what is $\operatorname{Cov}(X_{1}, X_{2})$?
tips: Multinomial counts are always NEGATIVELY correlated - the total n is fixed, so one cell can only grow at another's expense.
Do not divide by n: the covariance is $-n p_{i} p_{j}$, and -0.06 is the per-trial value planted as a distractor.
solution: For the multinomial, $\operatorname{Cov}(X_{i}, X_{j}) = -n p_{i} p_{j}$ for i not equal to j.

questions.question: For a hypergeometric distribution with $N = 20, K = 8$ and $n = 5$, what is $\operatorname{Var}(X)$?
questions.shortcut: Binomial variance $5(0.4)(0.6) = 1.2$ times the finite-population correction $15/19$ gives $18/19$.
tips: The hypergeometric variance is the binomial variance times $(N - n)/(N - 1)$, which is always below 1.
Quoting 1.2 (option a) is the trap for candidates who forget the correction factor entirely.

questions.question: A random variable has pmf $p(x) = \binom{8}{x} 3^{x} 5^{8-x}/8^{8}$ for $x = 0, 1, \ldots, 8$. What is $\operatorname{Var}(X)$?
questions.shortcut: Write $8^{8} = (3 + 5)^{8}$ to recognise $\text{Binomial}(8, 3/8)$; then $npq = 8(3/8)(5/8) = 15/8$.
tips: Whenever the denominator is $(a + b)^{n}$, the pmf is $\text{Binomial}(n, a/(a+b))$ in disguise.
The mean is 3 - option (a) is the mean planted in a variance question.

questions.question: X is $\text{Binomial}(n, p)$ with $\operatorname{E}(X) = 6$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X) = 4.2$. What is n?
questions.shortcut: $q = \operatorname{Var}$/mean = $4.2/6 = 0.7$, so $p = 0.3$ and $n = 6/0.3 = 20$.
tips: The ratio $\operatorname{Var}$/mean is exactly q for a binomial - the one division that unlocks every such question.
$\operatorname{Var}$ < mean signals the binomial; $\operatorname{Var}$ = mean would be Poisson and $\operatorname{Var}$ > mean negative binomial.

questions.question: X and Y are independent Poisson variables with means $\lambda_{1}$ and $\lambda_{2}$. The conditional distribution of X given $X + Y = n$ is
questions.shortcut: The Poisson sum is Poisson, and the ratio of the two pmfs collapses to a binomial with $p = \lambda_{1}/(\lambda_{1} + \lambda_{2})$.
tips: Conditioning a Poisson pair on their total always removes the scale and leaves a binomial split.
The same structure appears in Poisson thinning, where each event is independently labelled type 1 with that probability.
solution: $\operatorname{P}(X = k, X + Y = n) = e^{-\lambda_1} \lambda_{1}^{k}/k!$ times $e^{-\lambda_2} \lambda_{2}^{n-k}/(n-k)!$.
Dividing by the $\text{Poisson}(\lambda_{1} + \lambda_{2})$ pmf at n leaves $\binom{n}{k} p^{k} (1-p)^{n-k}$ with $p = \lambda_{1}/(\lambda_{1} + \lambda_{2})$.
So the conditional law is $\text{Binomial}(n, \lambda_{1}/(\lambda_{1} + \lambda_{2}))$, option (b).

questions.question: X and Y are independent geometric variables on {$1, 2, \ldots$} with success probabilities $p_{1}$ and $p_{2}$. Then $\min(X, Y)$ is geometric with success probability
questions.shortcut: $\operatorname{P}\!\left(\text{min > k}\right) = q_{1}^{k} q_{2}^{k} = (q_{1} q_{2})^{k}$, so the failure probability is $q_{1} q_{2}$ and success is $1 - q_{1} q_{2}$.
tips: Always take minima through the survival function: $\operatorname{P}\!\left(\text{min > k}\right)$ is a product for independent variables.
This is the discrete twin of "the minimum of independent exponentials has the sum of the rates".
solution: So $\min(X, Y)$ is geometric with failure probability $q_{1} q_{2}$.
Its success probability is $1 - q_{1} q_{2}$, option (c).

questions.question: X follows an exponential distribution with rate $\theta$. Then $\operatorname{Var}(X) > \operatorname{E}(X)$ if and only if
questions.shortcut: $1/\theta^{2} > 1/\theta$ reduces to $\theta < 1$.
tips: For the exponential the mean is $1/\theta$ and the variance is $1/\theta^{2}$, so the comparison is just 1 against $\theta$.
Nothing here is a general fact about exponentials - the answer depends entirely on the scale, which is the point of the question.

questions.question: X is $U(0, 1)$ and $Y = -2 \log X$. Then Y follows
questions.shortcut: $-\log X$ is $\text{Exp}(1)$, so $-2 \log X$ is Exp with mean 2.
tips: The probability integral transform in reverse: $-\log U$ is the standard exponential, and scaling multiplies the mean.
$-2 \log U$ is exactly the $\chi^{2}$ with 2 degrees of freedom, which is why it appears in random-number generation.
solution: $\operatorname{P}(Y > y) = \operatorname{P}\!\left(\text{-2 log X > y}\right) = \operatorname{P}(X < e^{-y/2}) = e^{-y/2}$.
This is the survival function of an exponential with rate $1/2$.

questions.question: X and Y are independent with X following $\Gamma(3, \lambda)$ and Y following $\Gamma(2, \lambda)$. What is $\operatorname{Var}(X/(X+Y))$?
questions.shortcut: $X/(X+Y)$ is $\text{Beta}(3, 2)$, whose variance is $6/(25 \times 6) = 1/25$.
tips: $\Gamma$ variables with a COMMON scale give a Beta ratio - this is the single most productive identity in the topic.
The mean of $\text{Beta}(3,2)$ is $3/5$, planted as option (c) for candidates who answer the wrong question.

questions.question: A density is $f(x) = k x^{2}/(1+x)^{6}$ for $x > 0$. What is k?
questions.shortcut: Beta of the second kind with $a = 3$ and $b = 3$; $B(3,3) = 1/30$, so $k = 30$.
tips: Read a and b straight off: the numerator exponent is a - 1 and the denominator exponent is a + b.
solution: Matching $x^{a-1}/(1+x)^{a+b}$ gives $a - 1 = 2$ and $a + b = 6$, so $a = 3$ and $b = 3$.

questions.question: For the density $f(x) = 30 x^{2}/(1+x)^{6}, x > 0$, what is $\operatorname{E}(X)$?
questions.shortcut: Beta of the second kind with $a = 3, b = 3$: the mean is $a/(b-1) = 3/2$.
tips: For Beta II the mean exists only when $b > 1$ and the variance only when $b > 2$ - always check before computing.
Reading the mean as $a/b = 1$ is the standard slip, planted as option (a).
solution: The density is Beta II with $a = 3$ and $b = 3$.
The mean of Beta II(a, b) is $a/(b - 1)$.

questions.question: X and Y are independent $N(0, 1)$ variables. What is $\operatorname{P}(\lvert X/Y\rvert < 1)$?
questions.shortcut: X/Y is standard Cauchy and $\operatorname{P}(\lvert C\rvert < 1) = (2/\pi) \arctan 1 = 1/2$.
tips: The ratio of two independent standard normals is standard Cauchy - worth recognising instantly.
By symmetry the answer is also just $\operatorname{P}(\lvert X\rvert < \lvert Y\rvert )$, which must be $1/2$ without any computation.
solution: X/Y follows the standard Cauchy distribution.

questions.question: X has density $f(x) = (1/2) e^{-\lvert x\rvert }$ on the whole line. What is $\operatorname{P}(\lvert X\rvert > 1)$?
questions.shortcut: $\lvert X\rvert$ is $\text{Exp}(1)$ for the standard Laplace, so $\operatorname{P}(\lvert X\rvert > 1) = e^{-1}$.
tips: Folding the standard Laplace gives exactly the standard exponential - the two halves each carry mass $1/2$.
Forgetting to double one tail gives $e^{-1}/2$, planted as option (b).

questions.question: X has density $f(x) = (1/2) e^{-\lvert x\rvert }$. What is $\operatorname{Var}(X)$?
questions.shortcut: Laplace with scale $b = 1$ has variance $2b^{2} = 2$.
tips: For $\text{Laplace}(0, b)$: $\operatorname{E}\lvert X\rvert = b, \operatorname{Var} = 2b^{2}$, kurtosis 6. The variance is twice the square of the scale, never the scale.
Reading $\operatorname{E}\lvert X\rvert = 1$ as the standard deviation gives option (a) - a very common confusion.
solution: The mean is 0 by symmetry, so $\operatorname{Var}(X) = \operatorname{E}(X^{2})$.

questions.question: If $\log X$ follows $N(0, 1)$, what is the median of X?
questions.shortcut: Medians pass through monotone transformations: the median of $\log X$ is 0, so the median of X is $e^{0} = 1$.
tips: Quantiles commute with strictly increasing maps; means do not.
The lognormal mean is $e^{1/2} = 1.6487$, planted as option (a) for candidates who answer with the mean.
solution: The median of $\log X$ is 0 because the normal is symmetric about its mean.
Exponentiating is strictly increasing, so the median of X is $e^{0}$.

questions.question: X is exponential with rate $\theta$. What is the maximum over $\theta$ of $\operatorname{P}(1 < X < 2)$?
questions.shortcut: With $u = e^{-\theta}$, the probability is $u - u^{2}$, maximised at $u = 1/2$ giving $1/4$.
tips: Substituting $u = e^{-\theta}$ turns an awkward optimisation over a rate into a one-line quadratic.
The maximising rate is $\theta = \log 2$, but the question asks for the maximum VALUE, not where it occurs.
solution: Put $u = e^{-\theta}$ in $(0,1)$: the expression is $u - u^{2}$, maximised at $u = 1/2$.

questions.question: X follows $N(\mu, \sigma^{2})$ with $\operatorname{P}(X < 20) = \operatorname{P}(X > 60)$ and $\operatorname{P}(X > 50) = 0.1587$. What is $\sigma$?
questions.shortcut: Symmetry gives $\mu = 40$; then 0.1587 means 50 is one standard deviation above 40, so $\sigma = 10$.
tips: $\operatorname{P}(X < a) = \operatorname{P}(X > b)$ always forces $\mu = (a + b)/2$ for a symmetric law - no tables needed.
0.1587, 0.0228 and 0.0013 are the one-, two- and three-$\sigma$ upper tails; recognising them saves the table lookup.

questions.question: What is the mode of the Beta distribution of the first kind with parameters 2 and 3?
tips: The Beta mode is $(a-1)/(a+b-2)$ and the mean is $a/(a+b)$; they coincide only when $a = b$.
The mean here is $2/5$, planted as option (a) - the question asks for the mode.
solution: The Beta $I(a,b)$ density is proportional to $x^{a-1}(1-x)^{b-1}$.
Setting its derivative to zero gives the mode $(a-1)/(a+b-2) = 1/3$.

questions.question: X is $U(-1, 1)$ and $Y = X^{2}$. What is the density of Y on $(0, 1)$?
questions.shortcut: $F_{Y}(y) = \operatorname{P}(\lvert X\rvert < \sqrt{y}) = \sqrt{y}$, so the density is $1/(2 \sqrt{y})$.
tips: For a non-monotone map always go through the CDF; differentiating a two-branch transformation directly is where marks are lost.
Both branches contribute, and here they exactly cancel the factor 2 from the density $1/2$ of $U(-1,1)$.

questions.question: X is $U(a, b)$ with mean 5 and variance 3. What is b?
tips: For the uniform the variance fixes the WIDTH and the mean fixes the midpoint; solve the two together.
Option (c) comes from treating $\sqrt{3}$ as a half-width, i.e. confusing the standard deviation with the range.
solution: The mean gives $(a + b)/2 = 5$, so $a + b = 10$.
The variance gives $(b - a)^{2}/12 = 3$, so $b - a = 6$.

questions.question: Which distribution has no moment generating function but has characteristic function $e^{-\lvert t\rvert }$?
questions.shortcut: $e^{-\lvert t\rvert }$ is the standard Cauchy characteristic function, and the Cauchy has no MGF because it has no mean.
tips: A characteristic function always exists; a moment generating function need not.
$e^{-\lvert t\rvert }$ is not differentiable at 0, which is exactly the analytic signature of an infinite first absolute moment.
solution: The standard Cauchy density $1/(\pi(1+x^{2}))$ has characteristic function $e^{-\lvert t\rvert }$.
Its integral for $\operatorname{E}\lvert X\rvert $ diverges, so no moment exists and the MGF is infinite for every t not equal to 0.

questions.question: The joint density is $f(x,y) = k(x + y)$ on the unit square. What is k?
questions.shortcut: The $\int x + y$ over the unit square is $1/2 + 1/2 = 1$, so $k = 1$.
tips: Split the integral by symmetry: each of x and y integrates to $1/2$ over the unit square.
The density value is not bounded by 1; do not "normalise" by guessing $1/2$.
solution: The double $\int (x + y)$ over $(0,1)^{2}$ is $\int x\,dx + \int y\,dy = 1/2 + 1/2$.

questions.question: For $f(x,y) = x + y$ on the unit square, what is $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)$?
questions.shortcut: $\operatorname{E}(XY) = 1/3$ and $\operatorname{E}(X) = \operatorname{E}(Y) = 7/12$, so $\operatorname{Cov} = 1/3 - 49/144 = -1/144$.
tips: The support is a rectangle but the density does not factorise, so X and Y are dependent - and here negatively so.
Compute $\operatorname{E}(X) = 7/12$ first; using $1/2$ by mistake makes the covariance vanish and lands on option (a).

questions.question: The joint density is $f(x,y) = 8xy$ on $0 < x < y < 1$. What is $\operatorname{E}(X \mid Y = y)$?
questions.shortcut: Given $Y = y$, the conditional density is $2x/y^{2}$ on $(0, y)$, which is $\text{Beta}(2,1)$ scaled to $(0,y)$: mean $2y/3$.
tips: Divide the joint density by the marginal and recognise the standard shape rather than integrating twice.
$y/2$ would be the answer for a UNIFORM conditional; here the conditional density is proportional to x, so the mean is pulled up to $2y/3$.

questions.question: The joint density is $f(x,y) = 2$ on $0 < x < y < 1$. What is $\operatorname{P}(X + Y < 1)$?
questions.shortcut: The region is the triangle with vertices $(0,0), (0,1), (1/2,1/2)$, of area $1/4$; times the density 2 gives $1/2$.
tips: With a constant density every probability is just (area of the region) x (the constant).
Forgetting to multiply by the density 2 gives $1/4$, planted as option (a).
solution: The support is the triangle $0 < x < y < 1$ of area $1/2$, on which the density is the constant 2.
The sub-region $x + y < 1$ within that triangle is the triangle $(0,0), (0,1), (1/2,1/2)$ of area $1/4$.

questions.question: For $f(x,y) = 2$ on $0 < x < y < 1$, the marginal density of X is
questions.shortcut: Integrate y from x to 1: $2(1 - x)$.
tips: Read the limits off the support: for a fixed x, y runs from x up to 1.
2x is the marginal of Y, not of X; the two are mirror images across the diagonal.

questions.question: X and Y are independent $\text{Exp}(1)$ variables. With $U = X + Y$ and $V = X/(X+Y)$, which statement is correct?
options: V is $U(0,1)$ and independent of U
questions.shortcut: $\Gamma(1,1)$ over $\Gamma(1,1)$ gives $V \sim \text{Beta}(1,1) = U(0,1)$, independent of the total $U \sim \Gamma(2,1)$.
tips: The Gamma-Beta engine: for independent Gammas with a common scale, the ratio to the total is Beta and is INDEPENDENT of the total.
U is $\Gamma(2,1)$, not $\text{Exp}(2)$ - the sum of two exponentials is not exponential.
solution: The Jacobian change of variables gives $f(u,v) = u e^{-u}$ on $u > 0, 0 < v < 1$.
This factorises into a $\Gamma(2,1)$ density in u and a constant density in v.
So V is $U(0,1)$ and independent of U, option (a).

questions.question: X and Y are independent $U(0,1)$. What is $\operatorname{P}(XY < 1/2)$?
questions.shortcut: Area below the hyperbola: $1/2 + \int_{1/2}^{1} 1/(2x)\,dx = 1/2 + (\log 2)/2$.
tips: Split the unit square at $x = 1/2$: below it the whole strip qualifies, above it only $y < 1/(2x)$.
The answer must exceed $1/2$ because the entire left half of the square already qualifies - that alone eliminates (c) and (d).
solution: For $x < 1/2$ the condition holds for all y, contributing area $1/2$.

questions.question: X is $U(-1, 1)$ and $Y = X^{2}$. Consider Statement I: $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y) = 0$. Statement II: X and Y are independent. Which is correct?
options: I is true, II is false
I is false, II is true
questions.shortcut: $\operatorname{E}(X^{3}) = 0$ by symmetry so the covariance vanishes, yet Y is an exact function of X, so they cannot be independent.
tips: Zero correlation means no LINEAR relation; it never rules out an exact non-linear one.
This is the standard counterexample to "uncorrelated implies independent" outside the bivariate normal.
solution: $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y) = \operatorname{E}(X^{3}) - \operatorname{E}(X)\operatorname{E}(X^{2}) = 0 - 0 = 0$, so Statement I is true.
Knowing X determines Y exactly, so $\operatorname{P}(Y = X^{2}) = 1$ and the two are strongly dependent.

questions.question: The joint pmf is $p(x,y) = (x + y)/21$ for x in {1,2,3} and y in {1,2}. What is $\operatorname{P}(X = 2 \mid Y = 1)$?
questions.shortcut: $\operatorname{P}(Y = 1) = (2 + 3 + 4)/21 = 9/21$ and $\operatorname{P}(X=2, Y=1) = 3/21$, so the ratio is $3/9 = 1/3$.
tips: Sum the row first: conditioning always divides by the marginal of the conditioning variable.
Option (a) is the JOINT probability - forgetting to divide by the marginal is the standard slip.

questions.question: For the joint pmf $p(x,y) = (x + y)/21$ on x in {1,2,3}, y in {1,2}, what is $\operatorname{P}(Y = 2)$?
tips: Check the total: the two rows give $9/21$ and $12/21$, which correctly sum to 1.
Options (b) and (d) are the same number written two ways, so read the option list before computing - only one form is offered here.
solution: The $y = 2$ entries are $(1+2), (2+2)$ and $(3+2)$, all over 21.
In lowest terms this is $4/7$, option (b).

questions.question: X follows $N(0, 1)$ and $Y = \lvert X\rvert$. What is $\operatorname{E}(Y)$?
questions.shortcut: The half-normal mean: $\operatorname{E}\lvert X\rvert = \sigma \sqrt{2/\pi} = \sqrt{2/\pi}$ for the standard normal.
tips: Memorise $\operatorname{E}\lvert X\rvert = \sigma \sqrt{2/\pi} = 0.7979 \sigma$ - it appears in mean deviation, in ranges and in half-normal questions.
$1/\sqrt{2 \pi}$ is the density height at 0, planted as option (c); the mean is twice that.
solution: $\operatorname{E}\lvert X\rvert = 2 \int_{0}^{\infty} x \phi(x)\,dx$ where $\phi$ is the standard normal density.

questions.question: X and Y are independent $\text{Exp}(1)$. Then X - Y follows
questions.shortcut: The difference of two independent exponentials with the same rate is the standard Laplace.
tips: The characteristic function is $1/(1-it)$ times $1/(1+it) = 1/(1+t^{2})$, which is exactly the Laplace.
$\lvert X - Y\rvert$ is $\text{Exp}(1)$ again; the SIGNED difference is Laplace. Option (a) confuses the two.
solution: The MGF of X - Y is $1/(1-t)$ times $1/(1+t) = 1/(1 - t^{2})$ for $\lvert t\rvert < 1$.
That is the MGF of the standard Laplace density $(1/2)e^{-\lvert x\rvert }$.

questions.question: The joint density is $f(x,y) = e^{-y}$ on $0 < x < y < \infty$. What is $\operatorname{E}(X)$?
questions.shortcut: X given Y is $U(0, Y)$ and Y is $\Gamma(2,1)$ with mean 2, so $\operatorname{E}(X) = \operatorname{E}(Y)/2 = 1$.
tips: Iterate the expectation: $\operatorname{E}(X) = \operatorname{E}[\operatorname{E}(X \mid Y)]$ turns a double integral into two one-line steps.
The marginal of Y is $y e^{-y}$, not $e^{-y}$ - reading it as $\text{Exp}(1)$ gives $\operatorname{E}(X) = 1/2$ and lands on option (a).
solution: The marginal of Y is $\int_{0}^{y} e^{-y}\,dx = y e^{-y}$, which is $\Gamma(2,1)$ with mean 2.
Given $Y = y$, the conditional density of X is $1/y$ on $(0,y)$, i.e. uniform, with mean $y/2$.

questions.question: For $f(x,y) = e^{-y}$ on $0 < x < y < \infty$, the marginal density of X is
questions.shortcut: Integrate y from x to $\infty$: $e^{-x}$.
tips: Read the limits from the support: for a fixed x, y runs from x upwards.
$x e^{-x}$ is the marginal of Y, obtained by integrating x from 0 to y - do not swap the two.

questions.question: The joint density is $f(x,y) = (2 \pi y)^{-1/2} \exp(-(x-y)^{2}/(2y)) e^{-y}$ for x real and $y > 0$. What is $\operatorname{Var}(X)$?
questions.shortcut: Hidden hierarchy: X given Y is $N(Y, Y)$ and Y is $\text{Exp}(1)$, so $\operatorname{Var}(X) = \operatorname{E}(Y) + \operatorname{Var}(Y) = 1 + 1 = 2$.
tips: Recognise the shape first: a normal kernel in x with mean y and variance y, multiplied by a marginal in y.
Use $\operatorname{Var}(X) = \operatorname{E}[\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Y)] + \operatorname{Var}(\operatorname{E}(X\mid Y))$; computing the marginal of X directly is far harder and is the trap.
solution: The first factor is the $N(y, y)$ density in x, and the second is the $\text{Exp}(1)$ density of Y.

questions.question: X and Y are independent $N(0,1)$. With $U = X + Y$ and $V = X - Y$, which statement is correct?
options: U and V are uncorrelated but dependent
questions.shortcut: (U,V) is jointly normal and $\operatorname{Cov}(U,V) = \operatorname{Var}(X) - \operatorname{Var}(Y) = 0$, and for a joint normal zero covariance means independence.
tips: Zero covariance implies independence only inside a JOINT normal - and a linear map of independent normals is joint normal.
$\operatorname{Cov}(X+Y, X-Y) = \operatorname{Var}(X) - \operatorname{Var}(Y)$, so the two are uncorrelated exactly when the variances are equal.
solution: (U,V) is a linear transformation of a bivariate normal, hence itself bivariate normal.
For a bivariate normal, zero covariance implies independence, option (b).

questions.question: (X, Y, Z) has joint density f. If $U = 2X, V = 2Y$ and $W = 2Z$, the joint density of (U, V, W) is
questions.shortcut: The Jacobian of the inverse map is $(1/2)^{3} = 1/8$, so the new density is f at the halved arguments divided by 8.
tips: Density transforms carry $\lvert J\rvert$ of the INVERSE map; stretching a variable must lower the density, never raise it.
Sanity check by integration: a factor 8 would make the total mass 64, not 1.
solution: The inverse map is $x = u/2, y = v/2, z = w/2$.

questions.question: The joint density is $f(x,y) = 6x$ on $0 < x < y < 1$. The marginal distribution of X is
questions.shortcut: Integrating y from x to 1 gives $6 \times (1 - x)$, which is the $\text{Beta}(2,2)$ density.
tips: The $\text{Beta}(2,2)$ density is $6 \times (1-x)$ - recognising the constant 6 identifies the law instantly.
$3x^{2}$ is the marginal you would get if the inequality ran the other way; check which variable is the upper limit.

questions.question: For $f(x,y) = 6x$ on $0 < x < y < 1$, what is $\operatorname{P}(X > 1/2)$?
questions.shortcut: X is $\text{Beta}(2,2)$, which is symmetric about $1/2$, so $\operatorname{P}(X > 1/2) = 1/2$.
tips: $\text{Beta}(a,a)$ is always symmetric about $1/2$ - no integration is needed for a median question.
If you do integrate, $\int_{1/2}^{1} 6 \times (1-x)\,dx = 1/2$ confirms it in one line.
solution: From the marginal, X follows $\text{Beta}(2,2)$ with density $6 \times (1-x)$.

questions.question: X given $Y = y$ is $\text{Poisson}(y)$ and Y is $\text{Exp}(1)$. What is the marginal $\operatorname{P}(X = k)$?
questions.shortcut: Integrating $e^{-y} y^{k}/k!$ times $e^{-y}$ gives $k!/(k! 2^{k+1}) = 1/2^{k+1}$: geometric on {0,1,$\ldots$} with $p = 1/2$.
tips: A Poisson whose rate is exponential becomes geometric - the $\Gamma$ integral does all the work.
Check the total: the sum of $1/2^{k+1}$ over $k \ge 0$ is 1, which confirms the normalisation.

questions.question: X given $Y = y$ is $\text{Poisson}(y)$ and Y is $\text{Exp}(1)$. What is $\operatorname{Var}(X)$?
questions.shortcut: $\operatorname{Var}(X) = \operatorname{E}[\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Y)] + \operatorname{Var}(\operatorname{E}(X\mid Y)) = \operatorname{E}(Y) + \operatorname{Var}(Y) = 1 + 1 = 2$.
tips: For a Poisson mixture both the conditional mean and the conditional variance equal Y, so the answer is $\operatorname{E}(Y) + \operatorname{Var}(Y)$.
Answering 1 forgets the variance of the mixing variable, which is exactly the over-dispersion the question is testing.

questions.question: X and Y are independent $U(0,1)$. What is the density of $Z = X + Y$ at $z = 1/2$?
questions.shortcut: The sum of two independent uniforms is triangular with density z on $(0,1)$, so $f(1/2) = 1/2$.
tips: The triangular density rises as z on $(0,1)$ and falls as 2 - z on $(1,2)$, peaking at 1.
The maximum value of the density is 1 at $z = 1$, so any answer above 1 is impossible; that rules out (d).
solution: The convolution gives $f_{Z}(z) = z$ for $0 < z < 1$.

questions.question: X is $U(0, 1)$ and $Y = -\log X$. Then Y follows
questions.shortcut: $\operatorname{P}(Y > y) = \operatorname{P}(X < e^{-y}) = e^{-y}$, the standard exponential survival function.
tips: $-\log U$ is the standard exponential - the basis of exponential random-number generation.
$-2 \log U$ would be $\text{Exp}(\text{mean }2)$; the factor in front is what sets the mean.
solution: Since X is uniform this equals $e^{-y}$ for $y > 0$.

questions.question: X and Y are independent with X following $\text{Exp}(\lambda)$ and Y following $\text{Exp}(\mu)$. What is $\operatorname{P}(X < Y)$?
questions.shortcut: The race between two exponentials is won by the faster rate: $\lambda/(\lambda + \mu)$.
tips: Competing risks: the probability that a given cause acts first is its own rate over the total rate.
If $\lambda$ is very large, X is tiny and $\operatorname{P}(X < Y)$ should tend to 1 - that eliminates (b) at once.

questions.question: The joint density is the constant c on the triangle $x > 0, y > 0, x + y < 2$. What are c and $\operatorname{E}(X)$?
questions.shortcut: The triangle has area 2, so $c = 1/2$; the centroid of a right triangle with legs 2 gives $\operatorname{E}(X) = 2/3$.
tips: A uniform density on a region is the reciprocal of its area, and its mean is the centroid.
The centroid of a triangle with vertices $(0,0), (2,0), (0,2)$ is at $(2/3, 2/3)$, not at $(1,1)$.
solution: The area of the triangle is $(1/2)(2)(2) = 2$, so $c = 1/2$.
By the centroid formula the mean of X is $(0 + 2 + 0)/3 = 2/3$.

questions.question: X takes non-negative integer values with $\operatorname{P}(X > x) = 1/2^{x+1}$ for $x = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$ What is $\operatorname{E}(X)$?
questions.shortcut: Tail sum: $\operatorname{E}(X) = \sum \operatorname{P}(X > x)$ = sum of $1/2^{x+1} = 1$.
tips: For a non-negative integer variable, $\operatorname{E}(X)$ is the sum of the tail probabilities starting at $x = 0$.
Here $\operatorname{P}(X > 0) = 1/2$, so X is geometric on {0,1,$\ldots$} with $p = 1/2$, whose mean $q/p = 1$ confirms the answer.

questions.question: A miner is at a fork with three doors, chosen with equal probability each time. Door 1 leads to safety in 2 hours, door 2 returns him to the fork after 3 hours and door 3 returns him after 5 hours. What is the expected time to safety?
questions.shortcut: Condition on the first door: $E = (2 + 3 + 5)/3 + (2/3)E$, giving $E = 10$.
tips: Set up a one-line recursion and solve; the returns restart the problem with the same expected value.
$10/3$ is the answer if you forget that two of the three doors send him back - it is the average travel time only.
solution: Conditioning on the first choice, $E = (1/3)(2) + (1/3)(3 + E) + (1/3)(5 + E)$.

questions.question: A fair coin is tossed until the first head appears. What is the expected number of tails?
questions.shortcut: The number of tosses has mean $1/p = 2$, so the number of tails is $q/p = 1$.
tips: Read the question carefully: tosses have mean $1/p$, failures before the first success have mean $q/p$.
The two differ by exactly 1, which is why 2 is planted as option (b).
solution: The number of tosses N is geometric on {1,2,$\ldots$} with mean $1/p = 2$.
The number of tails is N - 1.
Hence the expected number of tails is $2 - 1 = 1$, option (a).

questions.question: X is a non-negative integer variable with $\operatorname{E}(X) = 3$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X) = 4$. What is the $\sum x \operatorname{P}(X > x)$?
questions.shortcut: The identity gives $(\operatorname{E}(X^{2}) - \operatorname{E}(X))/2 = (13 - 3)/2 = 5$.
tips: Sum $x \operatorname{P}(X > x) = (\operatorname{E}(X^{2}) - \operatorname{E}(X))/2$ - the weighted twin of the plain tail-sum formula.
Compute $\operatorname{E}(X^{2}) = \operatorname{Var} + \text{mean}^{2} = 4 + 9 = 13$ first; using the variance alone gives the wrong answer.

questions.question: If $\operatorname{E}(X) = 2, \operatorname{E}(X^{2}) = 5$ and $\operatorname{E}(X^{3}) = 14$, what is the third central moment?
tips: $\mu_{3} = \mu_{3}' - 3 \mu_{1}' \mu_{2}' + 2 (\mu_{1}')^{3}$ - the one conversion worth memorising exactly.
A zero third central moment means the distribution is symmetric in the skewness sense; do not read it as "no moment".

questions.question: X is $U(0,1)$. What is $\operatorname{E}[\min(X, 1 - X)]$?
questions.shortcut: $\min(X, 1-X)$ is $U(0, 1/2)$, whose mean is $1/4$.
tips: The map x to $\min(x, 1-x)$ folds the unit interval onto $(0, 1/2)$ and doubles the density there.
The maximum possible value of the minimum is $1/2$, so its mean must be well below $1/2$ - option (a) is impossible.
solution: That is the survival function of $U(0, 1/2)$.

questions.question: Y is $\text{Bernoulli}(1/2)$. Given $Y = 0, X$ is $N(0,1)$; given $Y = 1, X$ is $N(2,1)$. What is $\operatorname{Var}(X)$?
questions.shortcut: $\operatorname{Var}(X) = \operatorname{E}[\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Y)] + \operatorname{Var}(\operatorname{E}(X\mid Y)) = 1 + \operatorname{Var}(2Y) = 1 + 4(1/4) = 2$.
tips: The variance decomposition splits into a within-group part and a between-group part; a mixture always has both.
Answering 1 uses only the within-group variance and ignores the separation between the two centres.
solution: $\operatorname{E}[\operatorname{Var}(X \mid Y)] = 1$ since both components have unit variance.

questions.question: What is the $\sum n (1/3)^{n-1}$?
tips: Differentiating the geometric series term by term turns $\sum x^{n}$ into $\sum n x^{n-1} = 1/(1-x)^{2}$.
The related sum of $n x^{n}$ is $x/(1-x)^{2} = 3/4$ here; read the exponent carefully.

questions.question: A random variable has $M(t) = (1/3 + (2/3) e^{t})^{5}$. What is $\operatorname{Var}(X)$?
questions.shortcut: Recognise $\text{Binomial}(5, 2/3)$: variance $npq = 5(2/3)(1/3) = 10/9$.
tips: $(q + p e^{t})^{n}$ is the binomial MGF; read n from the power and p from the coefficient of $e^{t}$.
The mean is $10/3$, planted as option (a) - the question asks for the variance.
solution: The MGF matches $(q + p e^{t})^{n}$ with $n = 5, p = 2/3$ and $q = 1/3$.

questions.question: X is $N(1, 4)$ and Y is $N(2, 9)$, independent, and $Z = 2X - Y$. What is $\operatorname{P}(Z > 5)$?
questions.shortcut: Z is $N(0, 25)$, so $\operatorname{P}(Z > 5) = \operatorname{P}\!\left(\text{standard normal > 1}\right) = 0.1587$.
tips: Linear combinations of independent normals are normal: means combine linearly, variances combine with the SQUARED coefficients.
Using $2 \times 4$ instead of $4 \times 4$ for the variance of 2X gives $\operatorname{Var} = 17$ and lands on a different tail.

questions.question: Which characteristic function belongs to a distribution with no finite mean?
questions.shortcut: $e^{-\lvert t\rvert }$ is the Cauchy characteristic function; it is not differentiable at 0, so no mean exists.
tips: A finite mean exists exactly when the characteristic function is differentiable at the origin.
(a) is $U(-1,1), (b)$ is Laplace and (d) is standard normal - all have every moment.
solution: $\sin t/t, 1/(1+t^{2})$ and $e^{-t^{2}/2}$ are the characteristic functions of $U(-1,1)$, Laplace and $N(0,1)$.
$e^{-\lvert t\rvert }$ is the standard Cauchy characteristic function and has a corner at $t = 0$.

questions.question: N is $\text{Poisson}(\lambda)$ and $X_{1}, X_{2}, \ldots$ are independent $\text{Bernoulli}(p)$ variables independent of N. The sum S of the first N of them follows
questions.shortcut: Compounding gives $\exp(\lambda(P_{X}(s) - 1)) = \exp(\lambda p (s - 1))$, the $\text{Poisson}(\lambda p)$ PGF.
tips: Poisson thinning: keeping each Poisson event with probability p leaves a Poisson with the rate multiplied by p.
The discarded events form an independent $\text{Poisson}(\lambda(1-p))$ - independence of the two streams is the classic follow-up.
solution: The PGF of S is $P_{N}(P_{X}(s))$ with $P_{X}(s) = q + ps$.
That is the $\text{Poisson}(\lambda p)$ PGF, option (b).

questions.question: N is geometric on {$1, 2, \ldots$} with success probability p, and $X_{1}, X_{2}, \ldots$ are independent $\text{Exp}(\theta)$ variables independent of N. What is the MGF of the sum Z of the first N of them?
questions.shortcut: Composing the geometric PGF with the exponential MGF gives $p \theta/(p \theta - t)$: Z is $\text{Exp}(p \theta)$.
tips: A geometric number of exponential steps is again exponential, with the rate multiplied by p.
Check at $t = 0$: any MGF must equal 1 there, which immediately kills option (d).
solution: The geometric PGF on {1,2,$\ldots$} is ps/$(1 - qs)$, and $M_{X}(t) = \theta/(\theta - t)$.
Substituting gives $p \theta/(\theta - t)$ divided by $(1 - q \theta/(\theta - t)) = p \theta/(p \theta - t)$.

questions.question: Which statement about a characteristic function $\phi$ is FALSE?
options: $\phi$ is unchanged by a change of origin
questions.shortcut: Shifting X to X + b multiplies $\phi$ by $e^{\text{itb}}$, so the characteristic function is not origin-invariant.
tips: Only the MODULUS of the characteristic function is unchanged by a shift; the function itself picks up a phase.
The other three properties hold for every characteristic function without exception.
solution: This differs from $\phi_{X}(t)$ unless $b = 0$, so statement (c) fails.

questions.question: A random variable has $M(t) = e^{t^2}$. What is $\operatorname{Var}(X)$?
questions.shortcut: The normal MGF is $\exp(\mu t + \sigma^{2} t^{2}/2)$, so $\sigma^{2}/2 = 1$ and the variance is 2.
tips: Match the coefficient of $t^{2}$: it is always half the variance, never the variance itself.
Reading $e^{t^2}$ as the standard normal MGF gives 1 and is exactly the trap; the standard normal MGF is $e^{t^{2}/2}$.
solution: Comparing $e^{t^2}$ with $\exp(\mu t + \sigma^{2} t^{2}/2)$ gives $\mu = 0$ and $\sigma^{2}/2 = 1$.

questions.question: A random variable has $M(t) = (1 - t/2)^{-3}$ for $t < 2$. What are its mean and variance?
questions.shortcut: $\Gamma$ with shape 3 and rate 2: mean $3/2$, variance $3/4$.
tips: The $\Gamma$ MGF is (1 - t/rate)^(-shape); read the shape off the exponent and the rate off the denominator.
Mean = shape/rate and variance = shape/$\text{rate}^{2}$, so the variance is the mean divided by the rate.

questions.question: U is $U(0,1)$ and $X_{n} = n$ times the indicator that $U < 1/n$. Which statement holds?
options: $X_{n}$ converges to 0 almost surely and in mean
$X_{n}$ converges to 0 almost surely but not in mean
$X_{n}$ converges to 0 in probability but not almost surely
questions.shortcut: For each fixed $U > 0$ eventually $1/n < U$, so $X_{n}$ goes to 0 pointwise, yet $\operatorname{E}(X_{n}) = n(1/n) = 1$ for every n.
tips: This is the standard counterexample showing almost sure convergence does not imply convergence in mean.
The mass escapes to $\infty$: the height n exactly cancels the shrinking probability $1/n$.
solution: For any fixed u in $(0,1), X_{n}(u) = 0$ once $n > 1/u$, so $X_{n}$ goes to 0 almost surely.
But $\operatorname{E}(X_{n}) = n \operatorname{P}(U < 1/n) = 1$ does not go to 0.
So convergence holds almost surely but not in mean, option (b).

questions.question: $A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots$ are independent events with $\operatorname{P}(A_{n}) = 1/n$. What is $\operatorname{P}\!\left(A_{n}\ \text{occurs infinitely often}\right)$?
questions.shortcut: The harmonic series diverges and the events are independent, so the second Borel-Cantelli lemma gives probability 1.
tips: Always compute the sum of the probabilities first: divergence plus independence gives 1, convergence alone gives 0.
Independence is needed only for the divergent case; the first lemma needs no independence at all.
solution: The events are independent, so the second Borel-Cantelli lemma applies.

questions.question: $A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots$ are independent events with $\operatorname{P}(A_{n}) = 1/n^{2}$. What is $\operatorname{P}\!\left(A_{n}\ \text{occurs infinitely often}\right)$?
questions.shortcut: The sum of $1/n^{2}$ converges, so the first Borel-Cantelli lemma gives probability 0.
tips: The first lemma needs only convergence of the sum; independence is irrelevant to it.
$\pi^{2}/6$ is the value of the sum, planted for candidates who confuse the sum with the answer - a probability cannot exceed 1.
solution: The sum of $1/n^{2}$ converges to $\pi^{2}/6$, which is finite.
By the first Borel-Cantelli lemma, $\operatorname{P}\!\left(A_{n}\ \text{infinitely often}\right) = 0$.

questions.question: $X_{n}$ follows $U(-n, n)$. The limiting distribution of $X_{n}$ is
options: uniform on the whole real line
questions.shortcut: $F_{n}(x)$ tends to $1/2$ for every fixed x, and the constant $1/2$ is not a distribution function.
tips: A limit of distribution functions is a distribution function only if it rises from 0 to 1; here the mass escapes to both infinities.
There is no uniform distribution on the whole line, so option (a) is not even a candidate.
solution: $F_{n}(x) = (x + n)/(2n)$ for $\lvert x\rvert \le n$, which tends to $1/2$ as n grows, for every fixed x.
The limit function is identically $1/2$, so it does not go to 0 at minus $\infty$ nor to 1 at plus $\infty$.

questions.question: $X_{n}$ converges in distribution to the constant c. Then
options: $X_{n}$ converges to c in mean square
questions.shortcut: Convergence in distribution to a CONSTANT is equivalent to convergence in probability to that constant.
tips: This is the one case where the weakest mode upgrades: a degenerate limit removes the usual gap.
Almost sure and mean-square convergence remain strictly stronger and do not follow.
solution: If $X_{n}$ converges in distribution to the degenerate law at c, then $\operatorname{P}(\lvert X_{n} - c\rvert > e)$ tends to 0 for every $e > 0$.
That is exactly convergence in probability.
The stronger modes need not hold, so the answer is option (a).

questions.question: For a sequence of independent random variables, the event that the series of the $X_{n}$ converges has probability
questions.shortcut: Convergence of the series is a tail event of an independent sequence, so Kolmogorov's zero-one law forces probability 0 or 1.
tips: Any event unchanged by altering finitely many terms is a tail event; convergence of a series is the standard example.
The law says the probability is 0 or 1, not which one - deciding that needs the three-series theorem.
solution: Changing finitely many $X_{n}$ does not affect whether the series converges, so the event lies in the tail $\sigma$ field.
For independent variables Kolmogorov's zero-one law makes every tail event trivial.
Hence the probability is 0 or 1, option (b).

questions.question: Weekly sales have mean 50 and variance 25. What lower bound does Chebyshev's inequality give for $\operatorname{P}(40 < X < 60)$?
questions.shortcut: The half-width 10 is $k = 2$ standard deviations, so the bound is $1 - 1/4 = 3/4$.
tips: Convert the interval to units of $\sigma$ first; the bound is always $1 - 1/k^{2}$.
0.9544 is the exact normal answer - Chebyshev makes no normality assumption and is far weaker.
solution: $\sigma = 5$, so the interval 40 to 60 is $\mu$ plus or minus $2 \sigma$.

questions.question: Chebyshev's inequality gives $\operatorname{P}(\lvert X - \mu\rvert < 3 \sigma)$ >=
tips: Chebyshev's three-$\sigma$ bound is $8/9$, while the normal three-$\sigma$ probability is 0.9973 - the gap is the price of assuming nothing.
$1/9$ is the bound on the TAIL, not on the central interval; read the direction of the inequality.
solution: Hence the central probability is at least $8/9$, option (b).

questions.question: X has mean 20, and the Chebyshev bound gives $\operatorname{P}(\lvert X - 20\rvert \ge 5) \le 0.16$. What is $\operatorname{E}(X^{2})$?
tips: Run Chebyshev backwards: the bound itself determines the variance when it is stated as an equality.
Do not stop at the variance - the question asks for the raw second moment, so add the square of the mean.
solution: Chebyshev gives $\operatorname{P}(\lvert X - 20\rvert \ge 5) \le \sigma^{2}/25$, and this equals 0.16.

questions.question: X is non-negative with $\operatorname{E}(X) = 2$. What upper bound does Markov's inequality give for $\operatorname{P}(X \ge 8)$?
questions.shortcut: Markov: $\operatorname{P}(X \ge a) \le \operatorname{E}(X)/a = 2/8 = 1/4$.
tips: Markov needs only non-negativity and the mean - no variance and no distributional shape.
The bound is useless whenever a is below the mean, since it then exceeds 1.
solution: Markov's inequality states $\operatorname{P}(X \ge a) \le \operatorname{E}(X)/a$ for non-negative X.

questions.question: A $\text{Bernoulli}(p)$ sample is used to estimate p. By Chebyshev's inequality, what is the smallest n guaranteeing $\operatorname{P}(\lvert \hat{p} - p\rvert < 0.1) \ge 0.9$ for every p?
questions.shortcut: $pq \le 1/4$, so the bound is $1 - 25/n \ge 0.9$, giving $n \ge 250$.
tips: Always use the worst case $pq = 1/4$ when p is unknown; that is what makes the guarantee uniform in p.
Chebyshev demands 250 where the central limit theorem needs only about 68 - a good illustration of how loose the bound is.

questions.topic: Laws of Large Numbers and Central Limit Theorem
questions.question: For 300 independent $U(0, 2)$ variables, what is the approximate value of $\operatorname{P}\!\left(\text{sum > 310}\right)$?
questions.shortcut: Mean 300 and variance $300(1/3) = 100$, so $z = 10/10 = 1$ and the tail is 0.1587.
tips: For $U(a,b)$ the variance is $(b-a)^{2}/12$; here that is $4/12 = 1/3$ per observation.
The standard deviation is 10, so 310 is exactly one $\sigma$ above the mean - recognise 0.1587 without a table.
solution: By the central limit theorem the sum is approximately $N(300, 100)$.

questions.topic: Laws of Large Numbers and Central Limit Theorem
questions.question: 1200 round-off errors are independent $U(-0.5, 0.5)$. What is the approximate value of $\operatorname{P}(\lvert \sum \rvert \le 20)$?
questions.shortcut: Variance $1200/12 = 100$, so 20 is two standard deviations and the central probability is 0.9544.
tips: The variance of $U(-1/2, 1/2)$ is exactly $1/12$, so n errors give variance $n/12$ - a very common exam setup.
The mean is 0 by symmetry, so the interval is symmetric and the two-sided normal value applies directly.

questions.topic: Laws of Large Numbers and Central Limit Theorem
questions.question: Statement I: the strong law of large numbers for independent and identically distributed variables requires a finite variance. Statement II: the sample mean of independent $\text{Cauchy}(0,1)$ variables converges to 0 in probability. Which is correct?
options: I is true, II is false
I is false, II is true
questions.shortcut: Kolmogorov's strong law needs only a finite mean, and the Cauchy sample mean is again Cauchy, so it converges to nothing.
tips: For identically distributed variables $\operatorname{E}\lvert X\rvert < \infty$ is necessary AND sufficient for the strong law.
The Cauchy mean has the same distribution as a single observation, so averaging achieves nothing at all.
solution: Statement I is false: a finite first absolute moment suffices, and no variance is needed.
Statement II is false: the average of n independent $\text{Cauchy}(0,1)$ variables is again $\text{Cauchy}(0,1)$.

questions.topic: Laws of Large Numbers and Central Limit Theorem
questions.question: For a random sample from $U(-3, 3)$, the large-sample distribution of $\sqrt{n}$ times the sample mean is
questions.shortcut: The variance is $36/12 = 3$, so $\sqrt{n} \bar{X}$ tends to $N(0, 3)$.
tips: The central limit theorem gives $N(0, \sigma^{2})$ for $\sqrt{n}(\bar{X} - \mu)$ - the limiting variance is $\sigma^{2}$, not $\sigma$ or $\sigma^{2}/n$.
The range 6 gives variance 3, not 9; squaring the half-width is the planted error.
solution: By the central limit theorem, $\sqrt{n}(\bar{X} - 0)$ tends in distribution to $N(0, 3)$.

questions.topic: Laws of Large Numbers and Central Limit Theorem
questions.question: $X_{1}, X_{2}, \ldots$ are independent and identically distributed with mean 0 and variance $\sigma^{2}$. Which normalisation converges in distribution to a non-degenerate limit?
questions.shortcut: Only the $\sqrt{n}$ scaling keeps the variance constant; the answer is the central limit theorem normalisation.
tips: Divide by n and you get the law of large numbers limit 0; divide by more than $\sqrt{n}$ and everything collapses to 0.
Divide by less than $\sqrt{n}$ and the variance explodes, so no limit law exists.
solution: This is constant in n exactly when $a = 1/2$.
So the sum divided by $\sqrt{n}$ is the right normalisation, option (b).

questions.topic: Laws of Large Numbers and Central Limit Theorem
questions.question: X is $\text{Poisson}(100)$. Using the central limit theorem without a continuity correction, $\operatorname{P}(X \le 110)$ is approximately
questions.shortcut: Mean and variance are both 100, so the standard deviation is 10 and $z = 10/10 = 1$.
tips: For the Poisson the variance equals the mean, so $\sigma = \sqrt{\lambda} = 10$ here.
Dividing by $\lambda$ instead of $\sqrt{\lambda}$ gives $\Phi(0.1)$, planted as option (b).

questions.question: $F(x)$ is 0 for $x < 0, \alpha x$ for $0 \le x < 1$ and 1 for $x \ge 1$. This is a valid distribution function if and only if
questions.shortcut: F only has to be non-decreasing and bounded by 1, so $\alpha \ge 0$ and $\alpha \le 1$; a jump at $x = 1$ is perfectly legal.
tips: A distribution function may jump; it need not be continuous, so $F(1-) < 1$ is allowed.
Insisting on $\alpha = 1$ is the trap - that would be the extra condition of continuity, which is not required.
solution: F is non-decreasing on $(0,1)$ exactly when $\alpha \ge 0$.
We also need $F(1-) = \alpha \le 1$, so that F does not exceed 1 before the jump.

questions.question: $F(x)$ is 0 for $x < 0, 1/4 + \alpha x$ for $0 \le x < 1$ and 1 for $x \ge 1$. What is the admissible range of $\alpha$?
questions.shortcut: Non-decreasing needs $\alpha \ge 0$ and $F(1-) = 1/4 + \alpha \le 1$ needs $\alpha \le 3/4$.
tips: Two conditions always: monotonicity fixes the lower end and $F(1-) \le 1$ fixes the upper end.
The value $1/4$ at $x = 0$ is an atom at the origin; that is allowed and does not force $\alpha$ to any single value.

questions.question: F is a continuous distribution function and X has that distribution. Then $-2 \log F(X)$ follows
questions.shortcut: $F(X)$ is $U(0,1)$, and $-2 \log U$ is exponential with mean 2.
tips: The probability integral transform turns any continuous variable into a standard uniform, after which standard tricks apply.
$-2 \log U$ is also $\chi^{2}$ with 2 degrees of freedom, which is the same as an exponential with mean 2.
solution: By the probability integral transform, $F(X)$ is $U(0,1)$.
For U uniform, $\operatorname{P}\!\left(\text{-2 log U > y}\right) = \operatorname{P}(U < e^{-y/2}) = e^{-y/2}$.
That is the exponential with mean 2, option (b).

questions.question: $F_{1}$ and $F_{2}$ are distribution functions. Which of the following need NOT be a distribution function?
questions.shortcut: A difference of distribution functions can be negative and does not tend to 1, so it fails.
tips: The product is the maximum of two independent variables and the second expression is the minimum; both are genuine.
The average is a 50-50 mixture, which is always a distribution function.
solution: The product is the distribution function of the maximum of two independent variables.
$F_{1} + F_{2} - F_{1}F_{2}$ is the distribution function of the minimum, and the average is a mixture.
$F_{1} - F_{2}$ tends to 0 at both ends and can be negative, so it is not a distribution function, option (d).

questions.question: $F(x) = 1/2 + (1/\pi) \arctan x$. What is $\operatorname{P}(X > 1)$?
questions.shortcut: This is the standard Cauchy distribution function; $F(1) = 1/2 + 1/4 = 3/4$, so the upper tail is $1/4$.
tips: $\arctan 1 = \pi/4$, so the $(1/\pi)$ factor makes the contribution exactly $1/4$.
$3/4$ is $F(1)$ itself, planted as option (c) for candidates who forget to subtract from 1.

questions.question: How many jump points does $F(x) = 1 - e^{-x}$ for $x \ge 0$, and 0 otherwise, have?
questions.shortcut: $F(0) = 0 = F(0-)$, so there is no jump anywhere; the exponential distribution function is continuous.
tips: A jump point is a value where $F(c)$ exceeds $F(c-)$; check the join of the pieces first.
The exponential density is discontinuous at 0, but the DISTRIBUTION FUNCTION is not - do not confuse them.
solution: So $F(0) = F(0-)$ and F is continuous everywhere else as well.
There are no jump points, option (a).

questions.question: Statement I: a distribution function must be continuous. Statement II: a distribution function must be right-continuous. Which is correct?
options: I is false, II is true
I is true, II is false
questions.shortcut: Discrete variables have jumps, so continuity fails; right-continuity is part of the definition.
tips: Right-continuity is a convention that fixes F at a jump to include the atom: $F(c) = \operatorname{P}(X \le c)$.
Every distribution function has at most countably many jumps, so continuity is the exception, not the rule.
solution: A Bernoulli variable has a distribution function with two jumps, so Statement I is false.
Right-continuity holds for every distribution function by definition, so Statement II is true.

questions.question: A fair die is rolled four times. What is the probability that the four outcomes are strictly increasing?
questions.shortcut: Each 4-subset of the six faces gives exactly one increasing order: $\binom{6}{4}/6^{4} = 15/1296$.
tips: "Strictly increasing" means choose the values, then the order is forced - so count subsets, never permutations.
$15/1296$ equals $5/432$; option (c) $5/324$ is the near-miss for a wrong denominator.
solution: There are $6^{4} = 1296$ equally likely outcome sequences.
A strictly increasing sequence is determined by its set of four distinct values: $\binom{6}{4} = 15$ of them.

questions.question: Eight people including one couple sit at random in a row. What is the probability that the couple sit together and neither of them is at an end?
questions.shortcut: Five interior adjacent slots, two internal orders, 6! for the rest: $5(2)(6!)/8! = 10/56 = 5/28$.
tips: Treat the couple as a block, then count only the block positions that avoid both end seats.
Ignoring the end restriction gives 7 blocks and the answer $1/4$, which is planted as option (a).
solution: The adjacent pairs that use no end seat are positions $(2,3)$ through $(6,7)$: 5 of them.
Each admits 2 internal orders and 6! arrangements of the others, so $5(2)(720) = 7200$ favourable orders.

questions.question: A point is chosen uniformly in the unit disc. What is the probability that it is nearer to the centre than to the boundary?
questions.shortcut: Nearer to the centre means $r < 1 - r$, i.e. $r < 1/2$, an area ratio of $(1/2)^{2} = 1/4$.
tips: For a uniform point in a disc, probabilities are ratios of AREAS, so they scale with the square of the radius.
Answering $1/2$ uses the radius ratio instead of the area ratio - the single most common error here.
solution: The distance to the boundary is 1 - r, so the condition is $r < 1 - r$, i.e. $r < 1/2$.
The favourable area is $\pi(1/2)^{2}$ and the total area is $\pi$.

questions.question: An integer is drawn uniformly from 1 to 100. What is the probability that it is divisible by 2, 3 or 5?
questions.shortcut: Inclusion-exclusion: $50 + 33 + 20 - 16 - 10 - 6 + 3 = 74$, so the probability is 0.74.
tips: Use $\operatorname{floor}$ division for each count; the triple intersection is the multiples of 30.
Adding $50 + 33 + 20 = 103$ alone exceeds 100, which shows immediately that the overlaps must be removed.
solution: Multiples of 2, 3, 5 number 50, 33, 20; of 6, 10, 15 number 16, 10, 6; of 30 number 3.

questions.question: A hand of 5 cards is dealt from a standard pack of 52. What is the probability that exactly two suits appear?
questions.shortcut: Choose the two suits, count all hands inside them, then subtract the two single-suit hands.
tips: "Exactly k" always means "at most k" minus the lower cases; $\binom{26}{5}$ alone counts one-suit hands too.
Option (a) is the at-most-two count and therefore over-counts; it is the standard trap.
solution: Choose the pair of suits in $\binom{4}{2}$ ways.
Hands drawn from those 26 cards number $\binom{26}{5}$, of which $2 \binom{13}{5}$ use only one suit.

questions.question: Two fair dice are thrown. What is P(sum = 7 given that at least one die shows 3)?
questions.shortcut: The conditioning event has 11 outcomes, of which $(3,4)$ and $(4,3)$ give a sum of 7.
tips: Count the conditioning set explicitly: "at least one 3" is $6 + 6 - 1 = 11$ outcomes, not 12.
Reporting $1/6$ answers the unconditional question and ignores the information given.
solution: The event "at least one 3" contains 11 of the 36 outcomes.
Of these, the sum is 7 for $(3,4)$ and $(4,3)$.

questions.question: X and Y are independent $U(0,1)$. What is P($\lvert X - Y\rvert < 1/4$ and $X + Y > 1$)?
questions.shortcut: The band $\lvert X-Y\rvert < 1/4$ has area $1 - (3/4)^{2} = 7/16$, and the map (x,y) to $(1-x,1-y)$ splits it in half.
tips: Exploit the symmetry of the square about its centre: it preserves the band and swaps the two sides of $x + y = 1$.
Multiplying the two probabilities as if independent gives $7/32$ by accident here, but the events are NOT independent - the symmetry is the honest route.
solution: The band $\lvert X - Y\rvert < 1/4$ has area $1 - (1 - 1/4)^{2} = 7/16$.
The reflection (x,y) to $(1-x,1-y)$ maps the band onto itself and exchanges $X+Y > 1$ with $X+Y < 1$.
So exactly half the band qualifies: $7/32$, option (b).

questions.question: Three dice are available: a fair one, one with faces 1,2,3,4,6,6 and one with faces 1,2,3,6,6,6. One is chosen at random and rolled twice, giving two sixes. What is the probability that the fair die was chosen?
questions.shortcut: Likelihoods $1/36, 4/36$ and $9/36$ give posterior weights 1 : 4 : 9, so the fair die has probability $1/14$.
tips: With equal priors the posterior is proportional to the likelihood alone - keep a common denominator and read the integers off.
The likelihood grows with the SQUARE of the number of sixes on the die, which is why the ratios are 1 : 4 : 9.
solution: $\operatorname{P}\!\left(\text{two sixes}\right)$ is $(1/6)^{2}, (2/6)^{2}$ and $(3/6)^{2}$ for the three dice, i.e. $1/36, 4/36$ and $9/36$.
The posterior weights are proportional to 1, 4 and 9, summing to 14.

questions.question: 30% of mail is spam. A word W appears in 60% of spam and 5% of legitimate mail. Two independent messages each contain W. What is the probability that both are spam?
questions.shortcut: $\operatorname{P}\!\left(\text{spam}\mid W\right) = 0.18/(0.18 + 0.035) = 36/43$, and independence squares it.
tips: Compute the posterior for one message first, then use independence - never apply Bayes to the pair at once.
$(18/43)^{2}$ forgets to normalise the numerator and is planted as option (d).
solution: For two independent messages the answer is $(36/43)^{2}$, option (a).

questions.question: An urn holds 3 balls; the number of white balls is 0, 1, 2 or 3 with equal prior probability. Two draws with replacement are both white. What is the probability that all three balls are white?
questions.shortcut: Likelihood $(k/3)^{2}$ gives weights 0, 1, 4, 9, so the answer is $9/14$.
tips: With replacement the draws are conditionally independent given k, so the likelihood is a clean square.
The $k = 0$ case has likelihood 0 and drops out; the weights 1 : 4 : 9 are the same pattern as the three-dice problem.
solution: The likelihood of two whites given k white balls is $(k/3)^{2}$.
Unnormalised posterior weights are $0, 1/9, 4/9$ and $9/9$, in the ratio 0 : 1 : 4 : 9.

questions.question: A bit 0 or 1 is sent with equal probability over a channel that flips each transmitted bit independently with probability 0.1. The same bit is sent twice and the receiver observes 1 then 0. What is the probability that the bit sent was 1?
questions.shortcut: Both hypotheses give the same likelihood $0.9(0.1)$, so the data are uninformative and the posterior equals the prior.
tips: When the likelihood is the same under every hypothesis, Bayes returns the prior unchanged - no computation is needed.
One agreeing and one disagreeing observation always cancel for a symmetric binary channel.
solution: The likelihoods are equal, so the posterior stays at $1/2$, option (c).

questions.question: The success probability p of a coin is $U(0,1)$. The coin is tossed twice and both tosses are heads. What is the probability that a third toss is a head?
questions.shortcut: Laplace's rule: $\operatorname{E}(p^{3})/\operatorname{E}(p^{2}) = (1/4)/(1/3) = 3/4$, which is $(k+1)/(n+2)$ with $k = n = 2$.
tips: The predictive probability is a ratio of moments of the prior, not the posterior mean of a single toss.
Laplace's rule of succession $(k+1)/(n+2)$ gives $3/4$ directly and is worth memorising.
solution: The posterior is proportional to $p^{2}$, so the predictive probability is $\operatorname{E}(p^{3})/\operatorname{E}(p^{2})$.
For a uniform prior these are $1/4$ and $1/3$.

questions.question: X is $\text{Binomial}(4, 1/3)$. What is $\operatorname{P}\!\left(X\ \text{is even}\right)$?
questions.shortcut: The parity formula gives $[1 + (1 - 2p)^{n}]/2 = (1 + 1/81)/2 = 41/81$.
tips: $\operatorname{P}\!\left(\text{even}\right) = [1 + (q - p)^{n}]/2$ comes from averaging the PGF at $s = 1$ and $s = -1$.
The answer must exceed $1/2$ when $p < 1/2$, which eliminates option (c) immediately.

questions.question: X is $\text{Poisson}(\lambda)$. What is $\operatorname{E}[X(X-1)(X-2)]$?
questions.shortcut: Factorial moments of the Poisson are pure powers: the r-th factorial moment is $\lambda^{r}$.
tips: Never expand $X(X-1)(X-2)$; recognise it as the third factorial moment and write $\lambda^{3}$ at once.
Option (a) is $\operatorname{E}(X^{3})$, the answer to the question candidates think they were asked.
solution: The r-th factorial moment of a Poisson is the r-th derivative of the PGF at $s = 1$.

questions.question: X is $\text{Poisson}(\lambda)$. What is $\operatorname{P}\!\left(X\ \text{is even}\right)$?
questions.shortcut: $[\operatorname{P}(1) + \operatorname{P}(-1)]/2$ with $\operatorname{P}(s) = \exp(\lambda(s-1))$ gives $(1 + e^{-2 \lambda})/2$.
tips: The even-part trick works for every PGF: average its values at $s = 1$ and $s = -1$.
Option (d) is $e^{-\lambda} \sinh(\lambda) = \operatorname{P}\!\left(X\ \text{odd}\right)$, the complement - read the parity asked for.

questions.question: X is geometric on {$0, 1, 2, \ldots$} with $p = 1/2$. What is $\operatorname{E}(X^{2})$?
questions.shortcut: Mean 1 and variance $q/p^{2} = 2$, so $\operatorname{E}(X^{2}) = 2 + 1 = 3$.
tips: On {0,1,$\ldots$} the geometric has mean $q/p$ and variance $q/p^{2}$ - both differ from the {1,2,$\ldots$} version.
Answering 2 gives the variance, not the second moment; the square of the mean must be added.
solution: For the geometric on {0,1,$\ldots$} with $p = 1/2, \operatorname{E}(X) = q/p = 1$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X) = q/p^{2} = 2$.

questions.question: For the negative binomial distribution counting failures before the r-th success, the ratio of variance to mean is
questions.shortcut: $\operatorname{Var}$/mean = $(rq/p^{2})/(rq/p) = 1/p$, which always exceeds 1.
tips: The negative binomial is always over-dispersed: the ratio $1/p$ is greater than 1 for every $p < 1$.
Compare with the binomial, where the ratio is $q < 1$, and the Poisson, where it is exactly 1.
solution: The mean is rq/p and the variance is rq/$p^{2}$.

questions.question: Comparing $\text{Hypergeometric}(N, K, n)$ with $\text{Binomial}(n, K/N)$, which statement is TRUE?
options: the hypergeometric variance is smaller whenever $n \ge 2$
questions.shortcut: The two differ by the factor $(N-n)/(N-1)$, which is below 1 as soon as $n \ge 2$.
tips: Sampling without replacement always reduces variability; the correction factor is never above 1.
At $n = 1$ the two coincide exactly, which is why the statement is restricted to $n \ge 2$.
solution: The factor $(N-n)/(N-1)$ is less than 1 exactly when $n \ge 2$.
So the hypergeometric variance is smaller, option (b).

questions.question: Twelve fair dice are thrown and $X_{i}$ counts the dice showing face i. What is $\operatorname{Corr}(X_{1}, X_{2})$?
questions.shortcut: The multinomial correlation is $-\sqrt{p_{1} p_{2}/(q_{1} q_{2})} = -(1/6)/(5/6) = -1/5$.
tips: The multinomial correlation does not depend on n at all - only on the cell probabilities.
$-1/6$ is $p_{1}$ itself and $-1/36$ is the product; neither is the correlation.
solution: $\operatorname{Cov} = -n p_{1} p_{2}$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X_{i}) = n p_{i} q_{i}$.

questions.question: X is $\text{Binomial}(2, 1/2)$ and Y is $\text{Binomial}(1, 1/4)$, independent. Is X + Y binomial?
questions.shortcut: $\operatorname{P}(S=0) = 3/16$ and $\operatorname{P}(S=3) = 1/16$, and no single p can produce both $q^{3} = 3/16$ and $p^{3} = 1/16$.
tips: Binomials add only when they share the SAME success probability; different p breaks the family.
Matching the mean gives $p = 3/8$ and matching the variance gives something else - the inconsistency is the proof.
solution: A $\text{Binomial}(3,p)$ would need $q^{3} = 3/16$ and $p^{3} = 1/16$, giving $q = 0.5724$ and $p = 0.3969$, which do not sum to 1.
So the sum is not binomial, option (c).

questions.question: X is $\text{Binomial}(10, p)$ with $\operatorname{P}(X = 3) = \operatorname{P}(X = 4)$. What is p?
questions.shortcut: The ratio condition $(n-k)p = (k+1)q$ with $k = 3$ gives $7p = 4q$, so $p = 4/11$.
tips: $\operatorname{P}(X=k+1)/\operatorname{P}(X=k) = [(n-k)/(k+1)][p/q]$; setting it to 1 gives the equal-probability condition in one line.
The answer must lie between $3/10$ and $4/10$ because the mode sits between 3 and 4 - a quick sanity filter.

questions.question: Events occur as a Poisson process of rate $\lambda$. Given exactly one event in (0, t], the time of that event is
questions.shortcut: Conditioning a Poisson process on one event in an interval makes its position uniform on that interval.
tips: The Poisson process has no memory and no preferred location, so a single conditioned point is uniform.
With n events in (0,t] the ordered times behave like the order statistics of n uniforms - the same principle.
solution: $\operatorname{P}(T \le s \mid N(t) = 1) = P$(one event in (0,s], none in (s,t])/$\operatorname{P}(N(t) = 1)$.
This equals $[\lambda s e^{-\lambda s}][e^{-\lambda(t-s)}]/[\lambda t e^{-\lambda t}] = s/t$.
So the time is $U(0, t)$, option (b).

questions.question: What is the expected number of rolls of a fair die needed to see all six faces at least once?
tips: Break the wait into stages: after k distinct faces the wait for a new one is geometric with mean $6/(6-k)$.
The answer is $n H_{n}$, which grows like $n \log n$ - never n or $n^{2}$.
solution: The waiting times for each new face are independent geometrics with means $6/6, 6/5, \ldots, 6/1$.

questions.question: X is uniform on {$1, 2, \ldots, 7$}. What is $\operatorname{Var}(X)$?
questions.shortcut: The discrete uniform variance is $(N^{2} - 1)/12 = 48/12 = 4$.
tips: Memorise $(N^{2}-1)/12$ for the discrete uniform on 1 to N; the continuous analogue would be $N^{2}/12$.
3.5 is the mean, planted as option (d).
solution: For the discrete uniform on 1 to $N, \operatorname{Var}(X) = (N^{2} - 1)/12$.

questions.question: X is exponential with rate 2. What is $\operatorname{E}(X \mid X > 3)$?
questions.shortcut: Memorylessness: $\operatorname{E}(X \mid X > a) = a + 1$/rate = $3 + 0.5 = 3.5$.
tips: The exponential forgets the past entirely, so the conditional expectation is the threshold plus the unconditional mean.
The answer must exceed 3 - option (d) 0.5 is the unconditional mean and cannot be right here.
solution: Given $X > 3$, the excess X - 3 is again $\text{Exp}(2)$.

questions.question: X follows $\Gamma$ with shape 3 and rate 2. What is $\operatorname{E}(1/X)$?
questions.shortcut: $\operatorname{E}(1/X)$ = rate/(shape - 1) = $2/2 = 1$.
tips: The inverse moment exists only when the shape exceeds 1; check that before computing.
$1/\operatorname{E}(X) = 2/3$ is planted as option (a) - Jensen's inequality guarantees $\operatorname{E}(1/X)$ is strictly larger.

questions.question: If $\log X$ follows $N(0, 1)$, what is $\operatorname{E}(X^{2})$?
questions.shortcut: $\operatorname{E}(X^{k}) = \exp(k \mu + k^{2} \sigma^{2}/2)$, so $\operatorname{E}(X^{2}) = e^{2}$.
tips: Read moments of the lognormal off the normal MGF at $t = k$; the exponent is quadratic in k, not linear.
$e^{2} - e$ is $\operatorname{Var}(X)$, planted as option (d) for a variance-versus-moment mix-up.
solution: $\operatorname{E}(X^{2}) = \operatorname{E}(e^{2 \log X}) = M(2)$ for the standard normal MGF.

questions.question: X follows Beta of the first kind with parameters a and b. What is $\operatorname{E}[X(1 - X)]$?
questions.shortcut: The ratio $B(a+1, b+1)/B(a,b)$ equals ab/$((a+b)(a+b+1))$.
tips: Any $\operatorname{E}[X^{r}(1-X)^{s}]$ for a Beta is a ratio of Beta functions - shift the parameters and divide.
Option (d) is $\operatorname{Var}(X)$, which is smaller; the check $a = b = 1$ gives $1/6$ for $\operatorname{E}[X(1-X)]$ but $1/12$ for the variance.
solution: With $a = b = 1$ this is $1/6$, matching $1/2 - 1/3$ directly, option (b).

questions.question: X follows $N(0,1)$. What is $\operatorname{E}(X^{4})$?
questions.shortcut: The standard normal moments are $1, 3, 15, \ldots$ : $\operatorname{E}(X^{2k}) = (2k-1)!!$ so $\operatorname{E}(X^{4}) = 3$.
tips: Memorise $\operatorname{E}(X^{2}) = 1, \operatorname{E}(X^{4}) = 3, \operatorname{E}(X^{6}) = 15$ - they run as the double factorials.
$\operatorname{E}(X^{4}) = 3$ is exactly why the normal kurtosis is 3 and the excess kurtosis is 0.

questions.question: X is standard Cauchy. Which of the following is NOT also standard Cauchy?
options: the average of X and an independent copy
questions.shortcut: The Cauchy is closed under reciprocal, sign change and averaging, but its square is a positive variable and cannot be Cauchy.
tips: The Cauchy is stable: any average of independent copies has exactly the same law.
$X^{2}$ is Beta of the second kind with parameters $1/2$ and $1/2$, supported on the positive half-line only.
solution: $1/X$ and -X are standard Cauchy by direct transformation.
The characteristic function $e^{-\lvert t\rvert }$ shows the average of independent copies is again standard Cauchy.
$X^{2}$ is non-negative, so it cannot be Cauchy, option (d).

questions.question: X follows $\text{Laplace}(0, b)$. Then $\lvert X\rvert$ follows
questions.shortcut: Folding the Laplace gives the exponential with the same scale b, i.e. rate $1/b$.
tips: Rate and scale are reciprocals - the most common place to lose a mark in this family.
This gives $\operatorname{E}\lvert X\rvert = b$ immediately, which is the Laplace mean deviation.
solution: $\operatorname{P}(\lvert X\rvert > x) = e^{-x/b}$ for $x > 0$ by symmetry of the Laplace density.
That is the exponential survival function with scale b.
So $\lvert X\rvert$ is exponential with rate $1/b$, option (b).

questions.question: X is $U(0,1)$. What is $\operatorname{Var}(X^{2})$?
questions.shortcut: $\operatorname{E}(X^{4}) - [\operatorname{E}(X^{2})]^{2} = 1/5 - 1/9 = 4/45$.
tips: Moments of a uniform on $(0,1)$ are $1/(k+1)$ - the whole computation is two fractions.
$1/12$ is $\operatorname{Var}(X)$, not $\operatorname{Var}(X^{2})$; squaring changes the spread.

questions.question: X and Y are independent $\text{Exp}(\lambda)$. What is $\operatorname{P}(X > 2Y)$?
questions.shortcut: Condition on Y: the $\int e^{-2 \lambda y} \lambda e^{-\lambda y}\,dy = 1/3$.
tips: For a ratio of independent exponentials, $\operatorname{P}(X > cY) = 1/(1+c)$ regardless of the common rate.
The rate cancels entirely, so any option depending on $\lambda$ would be wrong by inspection.

questions.question: What is the mode of the $\Gamma$ distribution with shape 2 and rate 1?
questions.shortcut: The $\Gamma$ mode is (shape - 1)/rate = 1.
tips: The $\Gamma$ mode is $(a-1)/\lambda$ for $a \ge 1$ and 0 for $a < 1$; the mean $a/\lambda$ is always larger.
The mean here is 2, planted as option (a) - a right-skewed density has its mode below its mean.
solution: The $\Gamma$ density is proportional to $x^{a-1} e^{-\lambda x}$.
With $a = 2$ and $\lambda = 1$ the mode is 1, option (b).

questions.question: For X following $N(\mu, \sigma^{2})$, what is $\operatorname{P}(\lvert X - \mu\rvert < 0.6745 \sigma)$?
questions.shortcut: $0.6745 \sigma$ is the quartile deviation, so the interval covers exactly the middle half.
tips: 0.6745 is the 75th percentile of the standard normal - the probable error constant.
0.6827 belongs to one $\sigma$, not to $0.6745 \sigma$; the two constants are routinely swapped.
solution: The 0.75 quantile of the standard normal is 0.6745.

questions.question: X follows Beta of the first kind with parameters 2 and 3, and $Y = X/(1 - X)$. What is $\operatorname{E}(Y)$?
questions.shortcut: The odds transform of Beta $I(a,b)$ is Beta II(a,b), whose mean is $a/(b-1) = 2/2 = 1$.
tips: $X/(1-X)$ converts Beta of the first kind into Beta of the second kind with the same parameters.
$\operatorname{E}(X)/(1 - \operatorname{E}(X)) = (2/5)/(3/5) = 2/3$ is the tempting wrong answer, planted as option (a).
solution: If X is Beta $I(2,3)$ then $X/(1-X)$ is Beta II(2,3).
The mean of Beta II(a,b) is $a/(b-1)$.

questions.question: X is $U(0,1)$. Compare $\operatorname{P}(X > 0.7 \mid X > 0.5)$ with $\operatorname{P}(X > 0.2)$.
questions.shortcut: The conditional probability is $0.3/0.5 = 0.6$, whereas $\operatorname{P}(X > 0.2) = 0.8$; the uniform is not memoryless.
tips: Only the exponential is memoryless among continuous laws - never assume it for a uniform.
If the uniform were memoryless the two numbers would agree; they do not, which is the whole point.

questions.question: For the lognormal distribution, the correct ordering of mode, median and mean is
questions.shortcut: They are $e^{\mu - \sigma^2}, e^{\mu}$ and $e^{\mu + \sigma^{2}/2}$, which increase in that order.
tips: The lognormal is right-skewed, so mode < median < mean - the standard order for positive skewness.
The three exponents $-\sigma^{2}, 0$ and $\sigma^{2}/2$ are strictly increasing, which settles the order without any numbers.
solution: The mode is $e^{\mu - \sigma^2}$, the median is $e^{\mu}$ and the mean is $e^{\mu + \sigma^{2}/2}$.
Since $-\sigma^{2} < 0 < \sigma^{2}/2$, the exponents increase in that order.

questions.question: X and Y are independent $\Gamma$ variables with shapes $a_{1}$ and $a_{2}$ and a common rate. Then X/Y follows
options: Beta of the first kind with parameters $a_{1}$ and $a_{2}$
Beta of the second kind with parameters $a_{1}$ and $a_{2}$
questions.shortcut: The ratio of independent Gammas with a common scale is Beta of the second kind, with mean $a_{1}/(a_{2} - 1)$.
tips: Ratio to the TOTAL gives Beta I; ratio to the OTHER variable gives Beta II. Keep the two apart.
The two are linked by $Y = X/(1-X)$: applying it to Beta $I(a_{1},a_{2})$ produces Beta II($a_{1}$,$a_{2}$).
solution: With a common scale, $X/(X+Y)$ is Beta $I(a_{1}, a_{2})$.
Writing $X/Y = [X/(X+Y)]/[1 - X/(X+Y)]$ converts it to Beta II($a_{1}, a_{2}$).

questions.question: X and Y are independent $\text{Exp}(1)$. What is $\operatorname{P}(X > 3Y)$?
questions.shortcut: $\operatorname{P}(X > cY) = 1/(1+c) = 1/4$ for $c = 3$.
tips: $Z = X/Y$ has density $1/(1+z)^{2}$, so $\operatorname{P}(Z > c) = 1/(1+c)$ - one formula covers every such question.
The exponential decay $e^{-3}$ is planted as option (d); the answer is algebraic, not exponential.

questions.question: X and Y are independent $N(0,1)$. What is $\operatorname{P}(X^{2} + Y^{2} \le 2 \log 2)$?
questions.shortcut: $X^{2} + Y^{2}$ is exponential with mean 2, so the probability is $1 - e^{-\log 2} = 1/2$.
tips: The $\chi^{2}$ with 2 degrees of freedom is exactly the exponential with mean 2 - the most useful special case in the family.
The threshold $2 \log 2$ is chosen so that $e^{-x/2}$ becomes exactly $1/2$.
solution: $X^{2} + Y^{2}$ has the $\chi^{2}$ distribution with 2 degrees of freedom, i.e. $\text{Exp}(\text{mean }2)$.
